sections.title: Introduction and Background
sections.tldr: Instant messaging usage surged to 4.3 billion users by 2020, accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic, with the Signal protocol becoming the most widely adopted encryption standard for secure messaging. Despite widespread deployment of end-to-end encryption in popular apps like WhatsApp and Signal, user understanding and trust in these security measures remains limited. (5 sources)
sections.text:
The landscape of instant messaging has experienced dramatic growth in recent years, with user adoption reaching 4.3 billion in 2020, representing a yearly increase of approximately 9% <Paper corpusId="238684360" paperTitle="(Afzal et al., 2021)" isShortName></Paper>. This growth was further accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic, which increased the use of instant messaging applications due to work-from-home policies implemented by most organizations <Paper corpusId="238684360" paperTitle="(Afzal et al., 2021)" isShortName></Paper>.

The Signal protocol has emerged as the most popular protocol in instant messaging, used by major platforms including WhatsApp, Facebook Messenger, and the Signal app itself <Paper corpusId="279391348" paperTitle="(Griggio et al., 2025)" isShortName></Paper>. Common instant messaging applications employ end-to-end encryption techniques during transmission to provide security and privacy to user data, with many claiming to use the Signal protocol for secure communication <Paper corpusId="238684360" paperTitle="(Afzal et al., 2021)" isShortName></Paper>. The scientific consensus recognizes the Signal protocol as technically sound, having been proven formally secure <Paper corpusId="279391348" paperTitle="(Griggio et al., 2025)" isShortName></Paper>.

However, despite the widespread deployment of end-to-end encryption, significant gaps remain in user understanding and trust. Even after WhatsApp's adoption of the Signal protocol and implementation of end-to-end encryption by default in 2016, user perceptions have been slow to change <Paper corpusId="279391348" paperTitle="(Griggio et al., 2025)" isShortName></Paper> <Paper corpusId="51983383" paperTitle="(Gerber et al., 2018)" isShortName></Paper> <Paper corpusId="201620872" paperTitle="(Dechand et al., 2019)" isShortName></Paper>. Studies have consistently shown that users do not trust encryption as currently offered, with many believing that their messages could still be read by third parties <Paper corpusId="279391348" paperTitle="(Griggio et al., 2025)" isShortName></Paper> <Paper corpusId="51983383" paperTitle="(Gerber et al., 2018)" isShortName></Paper>. This disconnect between technical security capabilities and user perceptions was highlighted during WhatsApp's 2021 privacy policy update, when 28.42% of users attempted to switch to SMS as an alternative, citing privacy and security concerns <Paper corpusId="279391348" paperTitle="(Griggio et al., 2025)" isShortName></Paper> <Paper corpusId="247788723" paperTitle="(Griggio et al., 2022)" isShortName></Paper>.

snippets: End-to-end (E2E) encryption is an effective measure against privacy infringement. In 2016, it was introduced by WhatsApp for all users (of the latest app version) quasi overnight. However, it is unclear how non-expert users perceived this change, whether they trust WhatsApp as a provider of E2E encryption, and how their communication behavior changed. We conducted semi-structured interviews with twenty WhatsApp users to answer these questions. We found that about half of the participants perceived that even with E2E encryption, their messages could still be eavesdropped, for example by hackers and other criminals, governmental institutions, or WhatsApp's employees and cooperation partners. Many participants correctly identified sender and recipient as weakest points after the introduction of E2E encryption, but misconceptions were still present. For instance, users thought that messages were transmitted directly between two devices without being forwarded or stored on a server, or interpreted 'end-to-end' as a temporally end of communication. The majority of users stated to mistrust WhatsApp and its E2E encryption and presumed image-related reasons for the cost-free implementation. While most participants did not change their communication behavior, they reported to use protection strategies such as sending sensitive content via alternative channels even after the introduction of E2E encryption.

snippets: With WhatsApp's adoption of the Signal Protocol as its default, end-to-end encryption by the masses happened almost overnight. Unlike iMessage, WhatsApp notifies users that encryption is enabled, explicitly informing users about improved privacy. This rare feature gives us an opportunity to study people's understandings and perceptions of secure messaging pre-and post-mass messenger encryption (pre/post-MME). To study changes in perceptions, we compared the results of two mental models studies: one conducted in 2015 pre-MME and one in 2017 post-MME. Our primary finding is that users do not trust encryption as currently offered. When asked about encryption in the study, most stated that they had heard of encryption, but only a few understood the implications, even on a high level. Their consensus view was that no technical solution to stop skilled attackers from getting their data exists. Even with a major development, such as WhatsApp rolling out end-to-end encryption, people still do not feel well protected by their technology. Surprisingly, despite WhatsApp's end-to-end security info messages and the high media attention, the majority of the participants were not even aware of encryption. Most participants had an almost correct threat model, but don't believe that there is a technical solution to stop knowledgeable attackers to read their messages. Using technology made them feel vulnerable.

snippets: In January 2021, WhatsApp announced an update to their privacy policy, sparking an outcry that saw millions of users install other messaging apps such as Telegram and Signal. This presented a rare opportunity to study users’ experiences when trying to leave the world’s most popular communication app. We conducted surveys in February and May with 1525 WhatsApp users from Mexico, Spain, South Africa, and the United Kingdom. Over a quarter wanted to switch at least part of their communication to other apps, but 74% of them failed to do so. By May, 27% had increased their use of other apps, and only 16% used WhatsApp less. Beyond network effects, users struggled with making informed choices of alternative apps and with differences in their design and functionality. We suggest messaging interoperability as an approach to alleviate switching costs and discuss implications for HCI research and competition regulation of digital services.

sections.title: Security Analysis and Formal Verification
sections.tldr: The Signal protocol has undergone extensive formal security analysis since 2020, with researchers using various mathematical frameworks including epistemic logic, Tamarin provers, and SPIN verification tools to confirm its security properties. These studies have validated the protocol's core security features while also revealing implementation vulnerabilities in real-world deployments. (10 sources)
sections.text:
The Signal protocol has been subject to comprehensive formal security analysis using multiple verification approaches. Researchers have employed epistemic logic to express security properties and analyze the protocol's behavior, finding that the protocol is indeed secure and contributing to security-by-design standards <Paper corpusId="246751465" paperTitle="(Kamkuemah, 2021)" isShortName></Paper>. The formal verification landscape includes extensive work using the Tamarin prover for modeling and verification, SPIN tools for composition protocol analysis, and various mathematical frameworks for proving security properties <Paper corpusId="272399516" paperTitle="(Li et al., 2024)" isShortName></Paper> <Paper corpusId="248948224" paperTitle="(Xiao et al., 2022)" isShortName></Paper>.

Multiple formal definitions and analyses have been conducted, with researchers generalizing and formalizing the double ratchet algorithms in the Signal protocol with security properties such as immediate decryption <Paper corpusId="257846977" paperTitle="(Lee et al., 2023)" isShortName></Paper> <Paper corpusId="199466153" paperTitle="(Durak et al., 2019)" isShortName></Paper>. Formal security analyses have treated the Signal protocol as a multistage authenticated key exchange protocol, demonstrating standard security properties that meet the protocol's security claims <Paper corpusId="257986538" paperTitle="(Alatawi et al., 2023)" isShortName></Paper>.

Recent research has focused on specific aspects of protocol security, including bidirectional authentication models that rigorously prove both symmetric and asymmetric ratchet phases satisfy strong authentication properties <Paper corpusId="279489812" paperTitle="(Xiao et al., 2025)" isShortName></Paper>. However, formal analysis has revealed gaps between theoretical security and practical implementation. Studies have shown that most deployed messaging apps fall far short of the security that their underlying mechanisms suggest, particularly regarding post-compromise security in multi-device settings <Paper corpusId="277667733" paperTitle="(Gegenhuber et al., 2025)" isShortName></Paper> <Paper corpusId="221992477" paperTitle="(Cremers et al., 2020)" isShortName></Paper>.

The research has also uncovered implementation vulnerabilities in real-world deployments, including account enumeration attacks possible in major messaging applications and severe privacy issues in contact discovery methods <Paper corpusId="277667733" paperTitle="(Gegenhuber et al., 2025)" isShortName></Paper> <Paper corpusId="221728040" paperTitle="(Hagen et al., 2020)" isShortName></Paper>. These findings highlight the ongoing challenge of translating formal security guarantees into secure practical implementations.

snippets: Protocol security in a composition protocol environment has always been an open problem in the field of formal analysis and verification of security protocols. As a well-known tool to analyze and verify the logical consistency of concurrent systems, SPIN (Simple Promela Interpreter) has been widely used in the analysis and verification of the security of a single protocol. There is no special research on the verification of protocol security in a composition protocol environment. To solve this problem, firstly, a formal analysis method for composition protocol based on SPIN is proposed, and a formal description of protocol operation semantics is given. Then the attacker model is formalized, and a message specification method based on field detection and component recognition is presented to alleviate the state explosion problem. Finally, the NSB protocol and the NSL protocol are used as examples for compositional analysis. It is demonstrated that the proposed method can effectively verify the security of the protocol in a composition protocol environment and enhance the efficiency of composition protocol verification.

snippets: Security and Privacy at Instant Messaging. Schrittwieser et al. were the first to investigate security and privacy issues in mobile instant messaging and VoIP applications, uncovering vulnerabilities such as account hijacking and number spoofing [24,(Schrittwieser et al., 2012). Beyond Over-the-Top (OTT) applications, similar security vulnerabilities have been identified in VoIP-based messaging solutions like VoLTE, VoWiFi and RCS (Gegenhuber et al., 2024)(Gegenhuber et al., 2024)(Tu et al., 2016)(Yang et al., 2024). In many cases, these vulnerabilities remained undiscovered for years due to proprietary clients and the lack of tooling for security experiments. We adopt a similar security testing approach to find vulnerabilities within WhatsApp, leveraging open-source tools to emulate a real client sending protocol queries to the server. In contrast, Hagen et al. (Hagen et al., 2020) demonstrated that large-scale account enumeration is possible in major messaging applications (e.g., WhatsApp, Signal) simply by automating interactions with the regular user interface. Beyond that, efficient account enumeration can also be achieved by using open-source clients to directly extract data from internal user APIs [14]

Cohn-Gorden et. al [9] provides a nice overview of the protocol as well as a formal security analysis of the triple Diffie-Hellman (X3DH) key agreement and the Double Ratchet (DR). The DR was initially analyzed in (Alwen et al., 2019). A new variant of the key agreement, called PQXDH, which includes PQ-KEM as been described and formally analyzed in [19]. Post-Compromise Security (PCS) was initially defined and analyzed in (Cohn-Gordon et al., 2019). Attacks on PCS in a multi device setting have been described in (Cremers et al., 2020)(Wichelmann et al., 2021). The entire conversation layer, potentially consisting of multiple sessions/devices of a user, has been analyzed in (Cremers et al., 2022) also with a focus on PCS and cloned devices.

snippets: We investigate whether modern messaging apps achieve the strong post-compromise security guarantees offered by their underlying protocols. In particular, we perform a black-box experiment in which a user becomes the victim of a clone attack; in this attack, the user's full state (including identity keys) is compromised by an attacker who clones their device and then later attempts to impersonate them, using the app through its user interface. Our attack should be prevented by protocols that offer post-compromise security, and thus, by all apps that are based on Signal's double-ratchet algorithm (for instance, the Signal app, WhatsApp, and Facebook Secret Conversations). Our experiments reveal that this is not the case: most deployed messaging apps fall far short of the security that their underlying mechanisms suggest. We conjecture that this security gap is a result of many apps trading security for usability, by tolerating certain forms of desynchronization. We show that the tolerance of desynchronization necessarily leads to loss of post-compromise security in the strict sense, but we also show that more security can be retained than is currently offered in practice. Concretely, we present a modified version of the double-ratchet algorithm that tolerates forms of desynchronization while still being able to detect cloning activity. Moreover, we formally analyze our algorithm using the Tamarin prover to show that it achieves the desired security properties.

snippets: — Contact discovery allows users of mobile messengers to conveniently connect with people in their address book. In this work, we demonstrate that severe privacy issues exist in currently deployed contact discovery methods. Our study of three popular mobile messengers (WhatsApp, Signal, and Telegram) shows that, contrary to expectations, large-scale crawling attacks are (still) possible. Using an accurate database of mobile phone number preﬁxes and very few resources, we have queried 10% of US mobile phone numbers for WhatsApp and 100% for Signal. For Telegram we ﬁnd that its API exposes a wide range of sensitive information, even about numbers not registered with the service. We present interesting (cross-messenger) usage statistics, which also reveal that very few users change the default privacy settings. Regarding mitigations, we propose novel techniques to signiﬁcantly limit the feasibility of our crawling attacks, especially a new incremental contact discovery scheme that strictly improves over Signal’s current approach. Furthermore, we show that currently deployed hashing-based contact discovery protocols are severely broken by comparing three methods for efﬁcient hash reversal of mobile phone numbers. sections.title: Implementation Vulnerabilities and Attack Vectors
sections.tldr: Research has revealed significant implementation vulnerabilities in Signal protocol deployments, including fake key attacks, account enumeration, contact discovery privacy breaches, and multi-device architecture weaknesses. These studies demonstrate that real-world implementations often fall short of the protocol's theoretical security guarantees. (5 sources)
sections.text:
Comprehensive security evaluations of Signal protocol implementations have revealed numerous vulnerabilities across different messaging applications. Studies of implementations such as Signal, WhatsApp, and Threema have concluded that none of the studied applications are infallible, with researchers identifying vulnerabilities that allow Signal servers to learn the contents of attachments, re-order and drop messages, and add or drop participants from group conversations <Paper corpusId="211266844" paperTitle="(Bahramali et al., 2020)" isShortName></Paper>.

Practical attack demonstrations have shown that consumer-facing messaging applications using the Signal protocol remain vulnerable to exploitation. Threat modeling frameworks have successfully identified vulnerabilities in applications with around 500 million users, with attacks successfully subverting application security and accessing confidential user data such as documents, media files, and audio memos <Paper corpusId="245881949" paperTitle="(Jain et al., 2021)" isShortName></Paper>.

Experimental research has demonstrated the feasibility of sophisticated attacks against Signal infrastructure. Researchers have successfully implemented fake key attacks, including both man-in-the-middle and impersonation attacks, by modifying Signal servers to hand out fake keys to clients, allowing attackers to decrypt and re-encrypt messages while remaining undetected <Paper corpusId="252968257" paperTitle="(Yadav et al., 2022)" isShortName></Paper>.

Privacy vulnerabilities in contact discovery and multi-device architectures have emerged as significant concerns. Large-scale crawling attacks remain possible against popular messengers, with researchers demonstrating the ability to query 10% of US mobile phone numbers for WhatsApp and 100% for Signal <Paper corpusId="280085658" paperTitle="(Gegenhuber et al., 2024)" isShortName></Paper> <Paper corpusId="221728040" paperTitle="(Hagen et al., 2020)" isShortName></Paper>. snippets: Our Signal infrastructure consisted of a server and five Signal clients (installed on Android mobile phones) for performing attacks and experimenting with defenses. The machine running the Signal server had Intel (R) Core (TM) i7-7700K CPUs @ 4.20 GHz, with 16 GB RAM. We used the open-source Signal server OWS 1.88 and clients using Signal-Android 4.23.4. Fake Key Attacks We modified the Signal server to perform fake key attacks (both MITM and impersonation). We added a client module to the server using the Signal client CLI 4 . It performs the standard ratcheting encryption done in normal Signal clients. We modified the server to hand out fake keys to clients. When the clients send encrypted messages to each other through the server, the server redirects the messages of the victim(s) to the client CLI module where the message is decrypted for the MKS to access it, and then re-encrypted and sent to the victim in the case of a MITM attack. Our experiment demonstrates that all fake key attacks described in Section 4.2 are possible in the current Signal server implementation. KTCA prototype: We used the transparency log prototype from CONIKS [11] and built the STR verification protocol on top of it. In addition, we modified the Android Signal client to add support for STR Verification Messages (SVM), which clients use to exchange STRs with their contacts to verify their consistency during every epoch. SVMs are routed through the Signal server in the same way that current Signal messages are communicated, but with an additional flag set in the message body. The receiving clients check this flag on every incoming message before displaying it in the chat window. We ran a simulation to measure the overhead of checking this flag on one million messages. The cost is 0.622 milliseconds per message before displaying the message in the chat window, which has a negligible impact on the user experience. AKM prototype We modified the Android Signal clients to support Anonymous Key Retrieval using the Tor Android Library. 5

snippets: Instant messenger security has been investigated since their early days. Schrittwieser et al. (Schrittwieser et al., 2012) analyzed attack vectors exploiting insufficient authentication in nine messenger applications. Back then, WhatsApp was found to be vulnerable to account hijacking, the unauthorized modification of the users' status pages, the unlimited delivery of unrequested SMS, and user account enumeration. A subset of attacks continued to exist over multiple years [9], (Hagen et al., 2020), [15], [19] and user account enumeration even become feasible for the more security-oriented messenger Signal (Hagen et al., 2020), [15]. With the advent of E2EE, Be'ery (Beery, 2024) and Gegenhuber et al. [8] discussed undesirable leaks of multi-device architectures, relevant for WhatsApp. For E2EE, one public key has to be maintained per device in the application's inventory and user behavior (i.e., addition or change of device) might be observed by changes in an account's public keys. Based on the delivering session, a receiver is also able to infer the sender's device issuing a message. Our research emphasizes that this also holds for Signal. Beyond, we discovered further privacy implications by exploiting delivery receipts as a side channel for WhatsApp and Signal.

sections.title: Forensic Analysis and Traffic Analysis
sections.tldr: Forensic investigators have developed network analysis techniques to identify Signal protocol activities through encrypted traffic patterns, while researchers have demonstrated that even privacy-focused messengers leak metadata that enables traffic analysis attacks for identifying users and group members. (5 sources)
sections.text:
Despite the Signal protocol's strong end-to-end encryption, forensic researchers have developed network analysis strategies to extract meaningful information from encrypted instant messaging traffic. Network forensic techniques can identify activities such as text, audio, video, and image messages as well as calls by examining payload patterns of encrypted traffic, and detailed analysis of trace files can help create lists of chat servers and IP addresses of involved parties <Paper corpusId="248436653" paperTitle="(Ahmad et al., 2022)" isShortName></Paper> <Paper corpusId="238684360" paperTitle="(Afzal et al., 2021)" isShortName></Paper>.

Traffic analysis attacks have proven effective against Signal protocol implementations, revealing that metadata privacy remains a significant vulnerability. Research has demonstrated practical traffic analysis attacks that enable adversaries to identify administrators and members of target messaging channels with high accuracy by merely monitoring encrypted traffic, without needing to leverage any software vulnerabilities <Paper corpusId="253098770" paperTitle="(Nelson et al., 2022)" isShortName></Paper> <Paper corpusId="211266844" paperTitle="(Bahramali et al., 2020)" isShortName></Paper>. These information leaks exist even in privacy-friendly messengers such as Signal and Threema <Paper corpusId="252992743" paperTitle="(Schnitzler et al., 2022)" isShortName></Paper>.

The research has led to the development of countermeasures and protocol variants designed to address these privacy concerns. Standard techniques such as adding cover traffic can degrade the effectiveness of traffic analysis attacks, and researchers have designed open-source countermeasure systems like IMProxy that can be used by messaging clients without requiring support from service providers <Paper corpusId="253098770" paperTitle="(Nelson et al., 2022)" isShortName></Paper> <Paper corpusId="211266844" paperTitle="(Bahramali et al., 2020)" isShortName></Paper>. Additionally, protocol variants like Deniable Instant Messaging (DenIM) have been developed to provide both the cryptographic guarantees of the Signal protocol and transport layer privacy for messages <Paper corpusId="253098770" paperTitle="(Nelson et al., 2022)" isShortName></Paper>.

sections.title: Protocol Extensions and Variants
sections.tldr: Researchers have developed several extensions and variants of the Signal protocol to address emerging challenges, with major focus areas including quantum-resistant implementations, specialized notification systems, audit-enabled group messaging, and comprehensive quantum-safe messaging frameworks. (5 sources)
sections.text:
The research community has developed various extensions and variants of the Signal protocol to address specific security and functionality requirements:

• **Quantum-Resistant Signal Protocol Variants**: Multiple research efforts have focused on creating quantum-safe replacements for the Signal protocol's traditional cryptographic foundations. These variants aim to replace vulnerable components like the DH-problem-based subprotocol and ECDH Curve25519 key exchange with quantum-resistant alternatives that can withstand attacks from quantum computers <Paper corpusId="268159652" paperTitle="(Goncalves et al., 2024)" isShortName></Paper> <Paper corpusId="268696153" paperTitle="(Sharma et al., 2023)" isShortName></Paper> <Paper corpusId="281093482" paperTitle="(Boras, 2025)" isShortName></Paper>.

• **Signal-Based Message Notification Protocol**: Researchers have developed specialized notification protocols for instant messaging applications that build upon the Signal protocol foundation, addressing the specific challenges of secure message notifications <Paper corpusId="271337498" paperTitle="(Almari et al., 2024)" isShortName></Paper>.

• **Audit-Enabled Group Messaging Protocol**: A novel variant has been designed to enable authorized audit access while maintaining privacy in group chat contexts. This implementation leverages the Signal protocol based on the Noise protocol framework and transforms group messaging into multiple two-way channels to preserve end-to-end encryption while facilitating auditing processes <Paper corpusId="275422918" paperTitle="(Tian, 2025)" isShortName></Paper>.

sections.title: Standardization and Interoperability Efforts
sections.tldr: The IETF has established standardization efforts including the MLS protocol (RFC 9420) for efficient group messaging and the More Instant Messaging Interoperability (MIMI) working group to enable cross-platform messaging between services like WhatsApp, Signal, and Telegram. These efforts aim to create industry standards while building upon the Signal protocol's proven security foundations. (4 sources)
sections.text:
The Signal protocol has gained widespread industry adoption across major messaging platforms, with Skype starting testing of "private conversations" using the Signal Protocol in January 2018, while Facebook Messenger and Google Allo also implemented the Signal Protocol for end-to-end encryption <Paper corpusId="236478360" paperTitle="(Okada et al., 2021)" isShortName></Paper>. This broad deployment spanning billions of users has established the Signal protocol as the only open-source E2EE protocol deployed at such massive scale <Paper corpusId="257757196" paperTitle="(Blessing et al., 2023)" isShortName></Paper>.

The Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) has taken significant steps toward standardizing secure messaging protocols. The IETF standardized the Messaging Layer Security (MLS) protocol as RFC 9420, which is intended to provide more efficient group communications than Signal and related protocols <Paper corpusId="257757196" paperTitle="(Blessing et al., 2023)" isShortName></Paper> <Paper corpusId="282757971" paperTitle="(Soler et al., 2025)" isShortName></Paper>. The MLS protocol efficiently expands end-to-end encryption to the context of group messaging, addressing limitations identified in Signal's group messaging capabilities <Paper corpusId="282757971" paperTitle="(Soler et al., 2025)" isShortName></Paper> <Paper corpusId="236478360" paperTitle="(Okada et al., 2021)" isShortName></Paper>.

In February 2023, the IETF created the More Instant Messaging Interoperability (MIMI) working group as their latest messaging interoperability standardization effort, dedicated to establishing the "minimal set of mechanisms" needed to allow contemporary messaging services to interoperate <Paper corpusId="257757196" paperTitle="(Blessing et al., 2023)" isShortName></Paper>. The MIMI protocol enables interoperable group messaging across otherwise isolated services such as WhatsApp, Signal, and Telegram by routing every MLS ciphertext through a central hub that timestamps messages and broadcasts them to all group participants <Paper corpusId="281153845" paperTitle="(Sarvaiya et al., 2025)" isShortName></Paper>. MIMI will extend MLS to address user discovery challenges and content formats for data exchange, with work expected to continue into 2024 <Paper corpusId="257757196" paperTitle="(Blessing et al., 2023)" isShortName></Paper>.

Several implementation approaches are being considered for widespread interoperability adoption. Meta has explicitly advocated for widespread adoption of Signal at the European Commission's stakeholder workshop, while hybrid solutions like Matrix-over-MLS have been proposed as part of the IETF's MIMI working group <Paper corpusId="257757196" paperTitle="(Blessing et al., 2023)" isShortName></Paper>. Despite using variations of the Signal protocol, major services including Signal, WhatsApp, Viber, and Facebook Messenger have developed different implementations and protocol versions, particularly for group communications <Paper corpusId="257757196" paperTitle="(Blessing et al., 2023)" isShortName></Paper>.

snippets: In recent years, instant messaging has become the main method of communication over the internet [1], which has sparked interest from the scientific community to analyse and improve their underlying security protocols. Endto-End Encryption (E2EE) (Mazunina et al., 2016) ensures that messages can only be decrypted by their intended recipients and not by any intermediate servers. Tools for anonymity have also been expanded: Signal's sealed sender [3] allows users to send messages such that the routing servers do not learn the identity of the sender. sections.title: User Experience and Authentication
sections.tldr: Research since 2020 has revealed significant usability challenges in Signal protocol authentication, with studies consistently showing poor user awareness and low participation rates in key verification procedures. While technical solutions like WhatsApp's implementation demonstrate robust cryptographic integration, the human factor remains the weakest link in maintaining authentication security. (3 sources)
sections.text:
User authentication in Signal protocol implementations faces substantial usability challenges that compromise security effectiveness. Studies have consistently shown that user awareness is very poor when it comes to authenticating keys in instant messaging applications, with usability research demonstrating that user awareness of participating in authentication procedures is quite low <Paper corpusId="273502190" paperTitle="(Teng et al., 2024)" isShortName></Paper>. Current solutions in the Signal protocol for key authentication to detect man-in-the-middle attacks depend on communicating pairs of users to compare fingerprints of their keys in an out-of-band manner, requiring users to perform this authentication ceremony periodically <Paper corpusId="273502190" paperTitle="(Teng et al., 2024)" isShortName></Paper>.

The reliance on user-mediated authentication creates fundamental security vulnerabilities. Research has revealed that modern messaging applications often rely on out-of-band communication to achieve entity authentication, with human users verifying and attesting to long-term public keys, but this approach leads to situations where authenticity guarantees are generally lost against active attackers, creating potential for man-in-the-middle attacks <Paper corpusId="243766464" paperTitle="(Dowling et al., 2021)" isShortName></Paper>. Analysis of Signal's user-mediated authentication protocol has shown it cannot be proven secure under formal threat models that capture active post-compromise entity authentication security <Paper corpusId="243766464" paperTitle="(Dowling et al., 2021)" isShortName></Paper>.

Despite these usability challenges, technical implementations of the Signal protocol demonstrate sophisticated cryptographic integration. WhatsApp's implementation successfully integrates symmetric and asymmetric cryptography through a comprehensive key exchange mechanism using Identity Key, Signed Pre Key, and One-Time Pre Key components, combined with the Double Ratchet Algorithm that generates unique session keys for each message <Paper corpusId="280531418" paperTitle="(Totnay et al., 2025)" isShortName></Paper>. However, the gap between technical security capabilities and user behavior in authentication procedures remains a critical weakness in real-world deployments.

snippets: Modern messaging applications often rely on out-of-band communication to achieve entity authentication, with human users verifying and attesting to long-term public keys. This is done primarily to reduce reliance on trusted third parties by replacing that role with the user. Despite a great deal of research focusing on analyzing the confidentiality aspect of secure messaging, the entity authenticity aspect of it, which relies on the user mediation, has been largely assumed away. Consequently, while many existing protocols provide some confidentiality guarantees after a compromise, such as post-compromise security (PCS), authenticity guarantees are generally lost, especially against an active attacker. This leads to potential man-in-the-middle (MitM) attacks. In this work, we address this gap by proposing a model to formally capture user-mediated entity authentication, as used by realworld protocols, that can be composed with any ratcheted key exchange. Our threat model captures active post-compromise entity authentication security. We demonstrate that the Signal application's user-mediated authentication protocol cannot be proven secure in this model and suggest a straightforward fix for Signal that allows the detection of an active adversary. Our results have direct implications for other existing and future ratcheted secure messaging applications.

sections.title: Widespread Adoption and Applications
sections.tldr: The Signal protocol has achieved widespread adoption across major messaging platforms, with implementations spanning from the dedicated Signal app to mainstream services like WhatsApp, Facebook Messenger, and Skype. This broad deployment demonstrates the protocol's versatility and establishes it as the de facto standard for secure messaging across billions of users worldwide. (1 source)
sections.text:
The Signal protocol has become the foundation for secure messaging across a diverse ecosystem of communication applications. One family of applications uses the Signal protocol directly, including the Signal app itself, WhatsApp, Facebook Messenger, Skype, and Riot <Paper corpusId="264935215" paperTitle="(Yadav et al., 2023)" isShortName></Paper>. Beyond these direct implementations, the protocol's influence extends to services that use proprietary implementations but follow the same core concepts, such as Wire and Viber <Paper corpusId="264935215" paperTitle="(Yadav et al., 2023)" isShortName></Paper>.

This widespread adoption represents a significant shift in the messaging landscape, where end-to-end encryption based on the Signal protocol has moved from niche privacy-focused applications to mainstream consumer services. The protocol's deployment across platforms with vastly different user bases and technical requirements demonstrates its flexibility and robustness as a security solution. From Meta's consumer-focused platforms to Microsoft's enterprise-oriented Skype, the Signal protocol has proven adaptable to various implementation contexts and security needs.

The broad implementation of the Signal protocol across these major platforms has effectively established it as the industry standard for secure messaging, creating a common cryptographic foundation that spans billions of users globally. This standardization has important implications for both security and interoperability, as it provides a shared technical baseline for secure communication across otherwise disparate messaging ecosystems.
